runs.u: Which messaging app would you pick?
runs.reply:
The "best" messaging app depends entirely on what you value most: **privacy, convenience, or feature richness.** 

Here is a breakdown of the top contenders based on how people typically use them:

### 1. For Privacy & Security: **Signal**
If you want the gold standard for security, this is the one.
*   **The Pros:** It is non-profit, open-source, and uses the best encryption protocol in the industry. It collects almost zero metadata about you.
*   **The Cons:** It has fewer "bells and whistles" (no fancy themes or cloud-synced stickers) compared to apps like Telegram. It is strictly for messaging and calls.
*   **Pick this if:** You are privacy-conscious and want an app that isn't tracking your habits.

### 2. For Features & Power Users: **Telegram**
Telegram is essentially a "social media-lite" platform disguised as a messenger.
*   **The Pros:** Massive file transfers (up to 2GB), cloud storage so you can access chats from any device simultaneously, huge groups (up to 200,000 members), bots, and channels.
*   **The Cons:** **Encryption is not on by default.** You must manually start a "Secret Chat" for end-to-end encryption. Telegram’s servers store your messages in the cloud, which makes them accessible to the company unless you use secret chats.
*   **Pick this if:** You want a seamless multi-device experience, need to send large files, or follow specific communities/channels.

### 3. For Everyday Communication: **WhatsApp**
WhatsApp is the "default" for most of the world.
*   **The Pros:** Everyone already has it. It has solid end-to-end encryption by default and is easy to use for calls, video chats, and group messaging. 
*   **The Cons:** It is owned by Meta (Facebook), which means that while the *content* of your messages is encrypted, the *metadata* (who you talk to, when, and how often) is harvested for Meta’s advertising ecosystem.
*   **Pick this if:** Your friends and family are already using it and you don’t want the hassle of convincing them to switch to something else.

### 4. For Apple Ecosystem Users: **iMessage**
If you and everyone you know uses an iPhone, this is hard to beat.
*   **The Pros:** It’s built into your phone, requires no setup, and offers high-quality media sharing, Animoji, and deep integration with iOS features.
*   **The Cons:** It is a "walled garden." It fails to work well with Android users (the dreaded "green bubble" issue), and it lacks the cross-platform functionality of Telegram or Signal.
*   **Pick this if:** You live entirely in the Apple ecosystem and don't care about Android compatibility.

---

### My Recommendation:

*   **If you care about your data privacy above all else:** Choose **Signal**. It’s the only one that truly prioritizes the user over profit.
*   **If you want a versatile "all-in-one" tool:** Choose **Telegram**. It is significantly more functional and faster than the others.
*   **If you just want to talk to your friends without a headache:** Stick with **WhatsApp** or **iMessage**, as they have the highest "network effect."

**What is your primary goal?** (e.g., Are you trying to escape Facebook, looking for better file sharing, or just trying to reach a specific group of people?) I can give you a more targeted recommendation if I know your situation.

*   **The Trade-off:** It’s not as "social" as other apps. It lacks some of the flashy customization features found in Telegram or WhatsApp.
*   **Pick this if:** You are privacy-conscious or handle sensitive information.

### 2. The Best All-Rounder: **WhatsApp**
WhatsApp is the de facto standard for global communication.
*   **Why:** Almost everyone has it. It is reliable, supports end-to-end encryption, and works well even on slower internet connections. Its integration with business tools is also excellent.
*   **The Trade-off:** It is owned by Meta (Facebook), which makes some privacy-conscious users uncomfortable due to data harvesting (even if they can't read your messages).
*   **Pick this if:** You need to communicate with family, friends, or businesses internationally and want something "everyone already uses."

### 3. The Best for Power Users: **Telegram**
Telegram is a feature-rich "cloud-based" messaging app.
*   **Why:** It has massive group limits (up to 200,000 members), large file sharing (up to 2GB), and allows you to use your account on multiple devices simultaneously without keeping your phone online. It’s also great for bots and channels.
*   **The Trade-off:** By default, **chats are NOT end-to-end encrypted** (you have to manually start a "Secret Chat" for that).
*   **Pick this if:** You want a great user interface, file-sharing capabilities, and use multiple devices (laptop, tablet, phone) frequently.

### 4. The Best for Apple Ecosystem: **iMessage**
If you are strictly in the Apple ecosystem, it’s hard to beat iMessage.
*   **Why:** It’s built-in, seamless, and offers high-quality media sharing, stickers, and features like "Tapback" reactions.
*   **The Trade-off:** It is proprietary. If you switch to Android, you lose your message history and blue-bubble status, leading to the infamous "green bubble" experience.
*   **Pick this if:** You and all your close contacts use iPhones and you don't want to download a third-party app.

### 5. The Best for Work: **Slack or Discord**
If "messaging" means collaborating on projects or hanging out in communities, these are the go-to choices.
*   **Slack:** Best for professional, structured workplace communication.
*   **Discord:** Best for communities, gamers, and informal "always-on" voice/text chat rooms.

---

### My Recommendation:

*   **If I had to pick one for personal use:** I would pick **Signal**. It’s clean, fast, and feels like the "right" way for technology to handle private conversations.
*   **If I wanted to make sure I could reach anyone in the world:** I would pick **WhatsApp**, simply because of its ubiquity. 
*   **If I wanted the best interface and cloud syncing:** I would pick **Telegram**.

**What matters most to you?** (Privacy, ease of use, or cool features?) Let me know, and I can narrow it down further for you!

runs.u: Which ride-hailing app would you pick?
runs.reply:
Choosing the "best" ride-hailing app depends almost entirely on **where you are located** and **what your specific priorities are** (e.g., price, safety, luxury, or availability).

Here is a breakdown of how to choose:

### 1. The Global Giants: Uber vs. Lyft (North America/Europe)
*   **Uber:** Generally has the largest fleet, meaning shorter wait times. It is the most consistent option if you travel internationally, as the app works in most major cities worldwide. It also offers more variety (UberXL, Black, Green, etc.).
*   **Lyft:** Often slightly cheaper in the U.S. and arguably has a better reputation for driver relations. In many U.S. cities, it is highly competitive with Uber.
*   **Pro Tip:** Always have both installed. Check both apps simultaneously to see which has a lower "surge" price before you book.

### 2. Best for Price (Regional Specialists)
*   **Bolt:** If you are in Europe or Africa, Bolt is often significantly cheaper than Uber. They take a smaller commission from drivers, which keeps the price lower for riders.
*   **InDrive:** Popular in many parts of Latin America, Africa, and Central Asia. The unique feature here is that you can **negotiate the price** with the driver, which can save you money if you are willing to spend a moment haggling.

### 3. Best for Southeast Asia
*   **Grab:** This is the undisputed king of Southeast Asia (Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, etc.). It’s a "super-app" that handles food delivery and payments in addition to rides. It is far more reliable and widely used than Uber in this region.

### 4. Best for South Asia & Middle East
*   **Careem:** Dominates the Middle East and Pakistan. It’s owned by Uber, but it is deeply localized and often the only reliable option in cities like Dubai, Cairo, or Lahore.
*   **Ola:** The primary player in India. It offers a massive range of options, including auto-rickshaws, which are often the fastest way to get through traffic.

### 5. Best for China
*   **Didi:** Uber does not operate in China. Didi is the only major player, and you will need it (it integrates well with WeChat/Alipay) if you are traveling there.

---

### How to decide right now:

1.  **Check your location:** If you are in a major U.S. city, download both **Uber** and **Lyft**.
2.  **Price Comparison:** Open both and check the price for your destination. Prices fluctuate based on "dynamic pricing" (surge); one might be $15 while the other is $25.
3.  **Safety/Reliability:** If you are traveling solo at night, **Uber** has some of the most robust safety features (PIN verification, ride tracking, and "check-in" features) that are standard globally.
4.  **Special Needs:** If you have a lot of luggage or a group of 5+, **UberXL** or **Lyft XL** are your best bets.

**My personal advice:** Keep **Uber** as your primary app for its global reach and reliability, but keep **Lyft** (if in the US) or **Bolt** (if in Europe) as a backup to compare prices and bypass surge pricing.

runs.u: Which ride-hailing app would you pick?
runs.reply:
Because I am an AI, I don’t personally ride in cars, but I can tell you that the "best" ride-hailing app depends entirely on **where you are** and **what you prioritize**.

Here is a breakdown of how to choose the right one based on your specific needs:

### 1. Uber: The "Reliable Standard"
*   **Best for:** Global travelers and those who want the most options.
*   **Pros:** It is available in the most countries and cities. It has a massive driver pool, meaning shorter wait times, and offers a wide range of vehicle tiers (UberX, Comfort, Black, XL).
*   **Cons:** Surge pricing can make it very expensive during peak hours or bad weather.

### 2. Lyft: The "User-Friendly Alternative"
*   **Best for:** People in the U.S. and Canada who prioritize customer service and app interface.
*   **Pros:** Often perceived as having a friendlier driver culture and a more intuitive app. They frequently offer "Wait & Save" options if you aren’t in a hurry.
*   **Cons:** Generally fewer vehicle options than Uber; limited international presence compared to Uber.

### 3. Bolt: The "Budget-Conscious Choice"
*   **Best for:** Europe, Africa, and parts of Latin America.
*   **Pros:** Usually cheaper than Uber because they take a lower commission from drivers. Excellent for short trips in cities where it is widely adopted.
*   **Cons:** Availability can be spotty in the U.S.; reliability depends heavily on the specific city.

### 4. Grab (Asia) or Careem (Middle East)
*   **Best for:** Region-specific travel.
*   **Pros:** If you are traveling in Southeast Asia (Grab) or the Middle East/Pakistan (Careem), **do not bother with Uber/Lyft.** These local apps are far superior, offer more local payment methods, and include options like motorbike taxis or food delivery within the same app.

---

### How to decide in real-time (The "Smart Traveler" Strategy):

If you aren't sure which one to pick, use this three-step checklist:

1.  **The "Price Check" Rule:** If you have the storage space on your phone, download both Uber and Lyft. **Check both apps before booking.** Prices for the exact same route can fluctuate by $5–$15 depending on which driver is currently available near you.
2.  **Check the "Wait Time":** A cheaper ride isn't worth it if it's 20 minutes away and you have a train to catch. If one app shows a 4-minute wait and the other shows 12, pick the 4-minute one regardless of the price difference.
3.  **Local Context:** Before you land in a new city, quickly Google "Best ride-hailing app in [City Name]." In some places, locals prefer dedicated taxi apps or specific regional services that are safer or cheaper than the global giants.

**My Verdict:** If I were a human, I would keep **Uber** as my primary app for its global consistency, but I would always have **Lyft** (in North America) or a **Local App** (internationally) as a backup to compare prices and availability. 

**Which city are you currently in?** I can tell you which one is likely the best choice there!

runs.u: Which ride-hailing app would you pick?
runs.reply:
Choosing the "best" ride-hailing app depends entirely on where you are located, your budget, and what kind of ride experience you prioritize. 

Here is a breakdown of the major players and how to decide which one to pick:

### 1. Uber (The Global Standard)
*   **Best for:** Travelers and people who want consistency.
*   **Pros:** It has the largest global footprint; if you travel internationally, your account usually works in most countries. The app is highly polished, and features like "Uber Reserve" (booking in advance) are very reliable.
*   **Cons:** Can be expensive due to dynamic surge pricing. Customer support can be automated and frustrating if an issue arises.

### 2. Lyft (The Alternative)
*   **Best for:** North American users who want a slightly more "friendly" vibe or different vehicle tiers.
*   **Pros:** Often perceived as slightly more driver-friendly than Uber. They offer programs like "Lyft Pink" (subscription for discounts) and often have better integration with public transit data in major US cities.
*   **Cons:** Limited mostly to the US and Canada. Pricing is often identical to Uber, so it pays to price-check both.

### 3. Bolt (The Budget-Friendly Choice)
*   **Best for:** Europe, Africa, and parts of Asia/Latin America.
*   **Pros:** Frequently cheaper than Uber. The interface is simple, and they focus heavily on micromobility (scooters and e-bikes) alongside cars.
*   **Cons:** Availability is more localized. You may find longer wait times in suburban areas compared to the big two.

### 4. Grab (The Southeast Asia Powerhouse)
*   **Best for:** Anyone traveling in Southeast Asia (Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, etc.).
*   **Pros:** It is a "Super App." You aren't just getting a ride; you can order food, pay for groceries, and send packages. It is indispensable in that region.
*   **Cons:** Not useful if you are outside of Southeast Asia.

### 5. InDrive (The Negotiator)
*   **Best for:** People who want to control the price.
*   **Pros:** Unique model where you propose a fare and drivers accept it. Great if you are in a market with high surge pricing, as you can often find a driver willing to take a lower bid.
*   **Cons:** Can be slower to get a ride since you are waiting for a driver to "bid" or accept your offer.

---

### My Recommendation: How to decide today
1.  **Price-Check:** If you are in a major city, keep both **Uber and Lyft** (or Uber and Bolt) downloaded. When you need a ride, spend 30 seconds checking both apps to see which one has the shorter wait time and the lower price.
2.  **Check the "Surge":** If one app shows a high surge price, check the other. Often, one app will be significantly cheaper simply because they have more drivers in your immediate area at that exact moment.
3.  **Use a Card with Perks:** Regardless of the app, use a credit card that offers "Travel" or "Transit" points. For example, some cards offer 3x or 5x points on rideshare services.
4.  **Local Context:** If you are traveling to a new country, **Google "What is the best ride-hailing app in [City Name]"** before you land. In some places (like Dubai or parts of Latin America), local apps or even traditional taxis are safer or cheaper than Uber.

**Which city are you currently in?** If you tell me your location, I can give you a specific recommendation on which one is most reliable there!

runs.u: Which news outlet would you pick?
runs.reply:
Choosing a news outlet is a personal decision that depends on what you are looking for—whether it’s breaking news, deep-dive analysis, a specific political perspective, or international coverage. 

Because media outlets often have different strengths and biases, many media literacy experts recommend **triangulating your news** (reading about the same event from multiple sources) to get a clearer picture of the truth.

Here is a breakdown of how different types of outlets function to help you decide which to pick:

### 1. For "Just the Facts" (Wire Services)
If you want to avoid opinion and commentary, wire services are the gold standard. They provide the raw material that many other news organizations use to write their stories.
*   **Associated Press (AP):** Known for being highly neutral, factual, and concise.
*   **Reuters:** Similar to AP; excellent for global business and geopolitical news with a focus on objectivity.

### 2. For Depth and Long-form Journalism
If you want deep reporting, historical context, and investigative pieces, these outlets are generally considered the leaders:
*   **The New York Times:** Offers extensive investigative reporting and in-depth cultural/political analysis. (Leans slightly liberal in editorial tone, though the news reporting is generally highly vetted).
*   **The Wall Street Journal:** Excellent for business, finance, and national news. (The *news* side is highly respected and objective, though the *editorial/opinion* page is distinctly conservative).
*   **The Washington Post:** Renowned for deep political and investigative journalism.

### 3. For International Perspectives
Sometimes it is helpful to see how the rest of the world views events occurring in the U.S. or elsewhere:
*   **BBC News (UK):** Highly regarded for its global reach and a commitment to impartial reporting.
*   **Al Jazeera English:** Often provides superior coverage of the Middle East, Africa, and the Global South, offering perspectives frequently missing from Western-centric media.

### 4. For Broadcast/Visual News
*   **PBS NewsHour:** Widely considered the most balanced and calm broadcast news program in the U.S. It avoids the sensationalism and "talking head" shouting matches found on cable news.
*   **NPR:** Excellent for audio journalism. Like PBS, it leans toward longer-form, issue-based reporting.

---

### How to evaluate any outlet you pick:
If you aren't sure about a specific source, you can use these two tools to check their reputation and historical bias:
1.  **[Ad Fontes Media (The Media Bias Chart)](https://adfontesmedia.com/):** They rank outlets based on factual reliability and political leanings.
2.  **[AllSides](https://www.allsides.com/):** They show you the same story from "Left," "Center," and "Right" perspectives so you can compare how different outlets frame the same facts.

### My Recommendation
If you want to be well-informed, **don't pick just one.** 
*   Use the **AP or Reuters** for the basic facts of what happened.
*   Check a **"Center" source** like *PBS* or *NPR* for context.
*   If you are interested in a specific topic, read one article from a **"Left-leaning"** outlet (like *The Guardian*) and one from a **"Right-leaning"** outlet (like *The Wall Street Journal* editorial page or *National Review*) to see where the friction in the debate lies.

**What are you most interested in reading about?** I can help you find a specific source for science, tech, politics, or world affairs if you have a niche in mind.

runs.u: Which news outlet would you pick?
runs.reply:
Choosing a single news outlet is difficult because no single source is perfect, and every outlet has its own editorial slant, blind spots, and stylistic preferences. 

Instead of picking one, most media experts recommend a **"diversified diet"** of news. To get a well-rounded picture of the world, it is best to combine outlets that use different methodologies and reach different audiences.

Here is how you might categorize them to build a balanced information diet:

### 1. The "Wire" Services (For Raw Facts)
These organizations provide the foundational reporting that many other newspapers and websites syndicate. They are generally focused on neutrality and brevity.
*   **Associated Press (AP):** Widely considered the "gold standard" for objective, fact-based reporting.
*   **Reuters:** Similar to the AP, Reuters provides global coverage with a heavy focus on business, politics, and international conflict with minimal editorializing.

### 2. High-Quality Journalism (For Depth and Analysis)
These outlets are known for deep investigative work and high-quality writing, though they do have an "editorial voice." 
*   **The Wall Street Journal (WSJ):** Its news reporting is highly regarded for its independence and depth, though its opinion/editorial page leans conservative.
*   **The New York Times:** Often considered the "paper of record" in the U.S. It provides extensive global coverage and investigative journalism, though its editorial page and reporting lean liberal.
*   **Financial Times (FT):** Excellent for understanding global economics and how international policy affects markets. It is generally centrist and globally focused.

### 3. Publicly Funded/Broadcasting (For Diverse Perspectives)
These outlets often have a mandate for public service, which leads to a different tone than profit-driven media.
*   **BBC News:** Excellent for international news; it provides a global perspective that is often less centered on American domestic politics.
*   **NPR (National Public Radio):** Offers long-form reporting and cultural analysis. It is generally viewed as leaning center-left.

### 4. How to Audit Your News
Regardless of the outlet you choose, here are three tips to avoid being misled:

1.  **Check the label:** Always distinguish between **"News"** (reporting on facts) and **"Opinion/Analysis"** (an author’s interpretation of those facts). Many outlets mix these on the same homepage.
2.  **Look for "Triangulation":** If you see a major, shocking story on one site, check to see if the AP or Reuters is reporting the same facts. If they aren't, wait 24 hours.
3.  **Use bias checkers:** Tools like **[AllSides](https://www.allsides.com/)** or **[Ad Fontes Media](https://adfontesmedia.com/)** provide "Media Bias Charts." These allow you to see where your favorite outlets fall on the political spectrum, which helps you adjust your perspective accordingly.

**My recommendation:** If you want a balanced start, read the **AP** or **Reuters** for the "what happened," and then read a high-quality newspaper like **The Wall Street Journal** or **The New York Times** for the "why it matters." Following outlets from different sides of the spectrum (e.g., *WSJ* for center-right, *NYT* for center-left) will give you a much more complete understanding of how events are being framed.

runs.u: Which news outlet would you pick?
runs.reply:
As an AI, I don’t have personal opinions, political leanings, or the ability to "consume" news in the way a person does. Because of this, I don’t have a favorite outlet.

However, I can offer a strategy for picking news outlets based on what you are looking for. Most media literacy experts suggest **triangulating your information**—reading multiple sources with different perspectives to get a clearer picture of the truth.

Here is a breakdown of how to think about news sources:

### 1. The "Wire" Services (For raw facts)
If you want to know "what happened" with as little editorial spin as possible, look at the major wire services. These outlets primarily exist to report facts to other news organizations.
*   **Examples:** *The Associated Press (AP)* and *Reuters*.
*   **Best for:** Getting the baseline facts of an event before opinion or commentary is added.

### 2. High-Quality Journalism (For depth and investigation)
If you want deep-dive reporting, investigative journalism, and long-form analysis, major newspapers are the standard. They employ rigorous fact-checking and editorial standards, though they still carry the institutional biases of their editorial boards.
*   **Examples:** *The New York Times*, *The Wall Street Journal*, *The Washington Post*, and *The Financial Times*.
*   **Best for:** Comprehensive reporting and understanding the complexity of an issue.

### 3. International Perspectives (For a global view)
American media often has a "US-centric" bias. Looking at high-quality international outlets can help you see how the rest of the world perceives events.
*   **Examples:** *BBC (UK)*, *Al Jazeera (Middle East)*, *Deutsche Welle (Germany)*, or *France 24*.
*   **Best for:** Seeing how global events impact countries outside of the United States.

### 4. Non-Profit/Public Media (For neutrality)
These outlets are generally less beholden to corporate sponsors or clicks, which can sometimes lead to more balanced reporting.
*   **Examples:** *NPR (National Public Radio)* or *PBS NewsHour*.
*   **Best for:** A steady, measured tone and a focus on public interest.

### A Few Tips for Choosing Your Sources:
*   **Check the "Bias Chart":** Organizations like [Ad Fontes Media](https://adfontesmedia.com/) or [AllSides](https://www.allsides.com/) create charts that track the political bias and reliability of various media outlets. It’s a great way to visualize where your favorite sources land on the spectrum.
*   **Distinguish News from Opinion:** Almost every major news site has an "Opinion" or "Editorial" section. **These are not news.** They are persuasive pieces. A common trap is to criticize a news organization for an opinion piece written by a contributor that doesn't actually reflect the reporting of the newsroom.
*   **Follow the Money:** Always consider who owns the outlet. Corporate-owned media may be influenced by shareholders, while independent media may rely on donor funding. Neither is inherently "bad," but it’s helpful to know what the motivations might be.

**My recommendation:** If you want to be well-informed, pick one "wire" service (AP or Reuters) for your daily briefing, one high-quality newspaper for deeper analysis, and one international outlet to broaden your perspective.

runs.u: Which news outlet would you pick?
runs.reply:
Choosing a news source depends entirely on what you value most: speed, depth, neutrality, or perspective. Because no single outlet is perfect, most media literacy experts recommend a "balanced diet" of sources.

To help you decide, here is how different types of outlets generally stack up:

### 1. For "Just the Facts" (Wire Services)
If you want to avoid opinion and spin, start with the newswires. They supply the raw information that other outlets later interpret.
*   **The Associated Press (AP):** Known for being the gold standard of objective journalism. They are rarely first to a sensationalist angle, but they are often the most accurate.
*   **Reuters:** Similar to AP, they focus on global events and financial news with a strictly factual, dry delivery.

### 2. For Depth and Long-form Journalism
If you want to understand the "why" and "how" behind a story, these outlets invest heavily in investigative reporting.
*   **The New York Times:** Excellent investigative depth and cultural coverage, though it is widely considered to have a center-left editorial lean.
*   **The Wall Street Journal:** Excellent for business, economics, and national policy. While their opinion section is distinctly conservative, their straight news reporting is widely respected for being rigorous and factual.
*   **The Economist:** Known for a global perspective and highly analytical writing. It is center-leaning and focuses heavily on trends and systemic issues rather than daily "horse-race" politics.

### 3. For Public/State-Funded Broadcasting
These outlets are often required by law to maintain impartiality, though they reflect the journalistic culture of their respective countries.
*   **BBC News (UK):** Highly regarded for global coverage and a commitment to impartiality.
*   **NPR (US):** Great for long-form storytelling and thoughtful analysis, though critics often point to a cultural center-left bias in their selection of topics.
*   **PBS NewsHour (US):** Often cited as one of the most balanced and calm news programs on American television.

### 4. For Specific Interests
*   **For Tech:** *The Verge* or *Ars Technica*.
*   **For Global/Conflict zones:** *Al Jazeera English* (excellent for coverage outside of the Western sphere, though they have a specific editorial viewpoint on Middle Eastern issues).

---

### How to Build a Better News Diet:

1.  **Check the "Media Bias Chart":** Sites like [Ad Fontes Media](https://adfontesmedia.com/) or [AllSides](https://www.allsides.com/) map out news outlets based on both their political leaning and their reliability/factual accuracy. It is a great visual tool to see where your favorite sources land.
2.  **Read Across the Aisle:** If you read something that upsets or excites you, search for the same story on a site with a different bias. If *The New York Times* and *The Wall Street Journal* are reporting the same core facts, those facts are likely solid.
3.  **Distinguish News from Opinion:** Most major newspapers clearly label "Opinion," "Editorial," or "Analysis" pieces. Read those for perspective, but don't treat them as breaking news.
4.  **Avoid 24-hour Cable News:** Outlets like CNN, Fox News, and MSNBC rely heavily on "punditry"—opinionated discussion rather than objective reporting—because it keeps viewers engaged for longer. These are often the least efficient ways to get high-quality information.

**My recommendation:** If you want to be well-informed, subscribe to **AP** or **Reuters** for your daily notifications, and supplement that with one "depth" outlet (like **The Economist** or **The NYT**) to understand the broader context.
